title: Gap Support
teaches: Gap Support as we trade it: a leader gaps up, price drifts back days or weeks later to the gap-up day's low (not the prior day's high) while the gap is still open, holds it or breaches it slightly, and closes back over it in the upper half of the test day; above a flat or rising 50-day and the 200-day; the stop sits a few cents under the test day's low; a third comes off at 3R, another at 5R, the rest on the 10-day or 21-day trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

steps: GPN, 2013. A quiet stock gaps up on 2013-10-02 on 11.5x volume. The gap-up low, 27.00, is the line.

The 200-day line
questions.answer: The gap-up day's low
questions.why: The gap-up day's low. That low is the line Gap Support defends, and Morales says a buyable gap-up should hold above it. The prior day's high is the gap-fill spot, a different level. On a true gap it sits below the line. The record-volume day's close is the High Volume Edge's line, and the 200-day is a filter for the test day.
questions.lesson_line: The line is the gap-up day's low.

wrong.The prior day's high: That is the gap-fill spot. It sits below the line, and it is not what we defend.
wrong.The record-volume day's close: That is the High Volume Edge's line, a different setup.
wrong.The 200-day line: The 200-day is a filter for the test day, not the line.

questions.simple: Gap Support defends the low of the gap-up day, not the prior day's high, which is only where the gap fills.

reasons: settled criteria card line, two facts

questions.q: The gap day itself is Gap Support.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The gap day itself is a PEG. A gap that is never revisited is nothing. The setup is the later test of the gap-up low.
questions.lesson_line: The gap day is a PEG. The later test is Gap Support.

questions.q: A Gap Support test day may close under the 200-day if the 50-day is rising.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The test day closes above the 200-day SMA, whatever the 50-day is doing. A test day that closes under the 200-day is off. Our rulebook bars longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, there is no Gap Support to buy.
questions.simple: False. A Gap Support test day must close above the 200-day, so a rising 50-day does not excuse a close under it.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The stop goes a few cents under the test day's ___.
questions.answer: low
questions.why: Low. The stop sits a few cents under the test day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the test day's low.

questions.q: In which market reading do we take only A+ gap tests?
choices: Orange
Green
Yellow
Red
questions.answer: Orange
questions.why: Orange. In an Orange market we take only A+ setups. Green is full risk per grade, Yellow is smaller and fewer, and Red is mostly cash and shorts. The market reading is a guide to how much risk to take.
questions.lesson_line: Orange means A+ only.

wrong.Green: Green is full risk per grade, not A+ only.
wrong.Yellow: Yellow is smaller and fewer, not A+ only.
wrong.Red: Red is mostly cash and shorts, not A+ only.

questions.simple: Orange means only A+ setups. Green is full risk, Yellow is smaller and fewer, and Red is mostly cash.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (market reading, A10)

questions.q: Gap Support buys are limit orders set just under the line.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Our rulebook says entries are market orders. The Gap Support card agrees: the close entry is a market order near the close.
questions.lesson_line: Entries are market orders.
questions.simple: False. We buy Gap Support with market orders, not limit orders set under the line.

questions.q: What makes an up gap a true gap?
choices: Its low is above the prior high
The open is above the prior close
Volume doubles the average
The close is above the day's open
questions.answer: Its low is above the prior high
questions.why: Its low is above the prior day's high. A true gap means the whole gap day trades above the prior day's high. An open above the prior close is not enough, because the low can fall back into the prior day's range.
questions.lesson_line: A true gap leaves a hole above yesterday's high.

wrong.The open is above the prior close: That can happen with the low back inside the prior day's range; a true gap needs more.
wrong.The close is above the day's open: A close above the open says nothing about a hole.

questions.simple: A true gap means the day's low stays above the prior day's high, so the whole day trades above it.

reasons: one cited fact only (a proposed card criterion)

questions.q: When is the gap still open?
choices: No close at or under prior high
No trade under the gap-up low
Green closes every day since
Volume stays above average since
questions.answer: No close at or under prior high
questions.why: No close at or under the prior day's high since the gap day. That prior high is the gap-fill spot. One close at or under it means the gap filled and the setup is dead.
questions.lesson_line: Open means no close back at the gap-fill spot.

wrong.No trade under the gap-up low: A slight trade under the gap-up low is allowed. The gap-fill spot is the test.
wrong.Green closes every day since: Only a close at or under the prior day's high ends it. The color of the days does not matter.
wrong.Volume stays above average since: Volume does not decide whether a gap is open.

questions.simple: The gap stays open while no day has closed at or under the prior day's high since the gap day.

reasons: fixed before; the card's wording on closes inside the gap overlaps the failed-gap line (see conflicts)

questions.q: A close at or under the prior day's high means the gap filled and the setup is dead.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A close at or under the gap-fill spot means the gap filled and the setup is dead. Buyable gap-ups do not close their gaps.
questions.lesson_line: A close at the gap-fill spot kills it.

questions.q: A gap out of a downtrend, under a falling 50-day, is not Gap Support.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. No downtrend gaps: the gap day closes above a flat or rising 50-day. Morales: not while the stock is in a downtrend.
questions.lesson_line: No downtrend gaps.

questions.q: Why not put the stop under the gap-fill spot?
choices: It is usually far from the entry
It is too close to the entry
It sits above the gap-up day's low
It moves up as the stock rises
questions.answer: It is usually far from the entry
questions.why: It is far from the entry. A stop under the gap-fill spot is a median 6% away, only 12% within 3%, and it wins less often per R. If the honest stop is more than about 3% away, we size down or skip. Our stop goes a few cents under the test day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Stop under the test day's low, not the fill spot.

wrong.It sits above the gap-up day's low: On a true gap the gap-fill spot sits under the gap-up day's low, not above it.
wrong.It is too close to the entry: It is the opposite. A stop under the gap-fill spot is far from the entry.
wrong.It moves up as the stock rises: The gap-fill spot is the prior day's high. It is a fixed price, not a trailing level.

questions.simple: A stop under the gap-fill spot sits a median 6% away, which is far, and it wins less often per R.

deeper.trap: A far stop feels like more room, but the size comes from the stop. The shares shrink as the distance grows. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade and do not pull the stop in.

reasons: a research statistic (median 6%, 12% within 3%) that can change

questions.q: Heavy-volume selling into the line is a warning, and a quiet pullback is the version traders like best.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Heavy-volume selling into the line is a warning, not a rule. A quiet pullback on lighter volume is the version traders like best.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy selling into the line is a warning. A quiet pullback is the version traders like best.
questions.simple: True. Heavy-volume selling into the line is a warning, and a quiet pullback on lighter volume is the version traders like best.

reasons: proposed criterion on the card, pending the owner's review

questions.q: Where should the test day close?
choices: Back over the line, in the upper half
Right at the day's low
Under the line, in the lower half
At the prior day's high
questions.answer: Back over the line, in the upper half
questions.why: Back over the line, in the upper half of its range. A lower wick or a hammer is the look.
questions.lesson_line: A lower wick and a strong close at the line.

wrong.Right at the day's low: A close at the low is a day still falling.
wrong.Under the line, in the lower half: A close under the line is not a hold.
wrong.At the prior day's high: The prior day's high is the gap-fill spot, far below the line.

questions.q: Gap Support is bought at full size, at one price, with one stop, and not built up in pieces.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We buy the full size at one price with one stop, and we do not add. A gap test is a new trade, not an add.
questions.lesson_line: One buy, one price, one stop.
questions.simple: True. We buy the whole size at once, at one price with one stop, and we never add to it.

questions.q: The stop sits in a real stop order with the broker, and it only moves up.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The card calls for a real stop order with the broker. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule: when a gap goes through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: A real stop order, and it only moves up.
questions.simple: True. The stop is a real order with the broker, and it only moves up, never down or wider.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B20)

questions.q: Gap-up low 53.03, test-day low 52.45. How deep is the breach, in percent?
questions.why: 1.1. Take the gap-up low minus the test-day low, then divide by the gap-up low, and give it as a percent. ILMN's slight undercut was this deep, 1.1% under 53.03, and the day closed at 94% of its range.
questions.lesson_line: Breach depth is the dip under the line, over the line.
questions.simple: Subtract the test-day low from the gap-up low, then divide by the gap-up low, to get about 1.1 percent.

deeper.example: ILMN: the test day's low broke the 53.03 line by 1.1%, yet the day closed at 94% of its range. The scan bought 53.27 with the stop at 52.40, and the best the trade reached was 18.6R.

questions.q: Bought at 25.10 with the stop at 24.71. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 26.27. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill. The first trim is a third at 3R. AKAM ran to 30.4R from these levels.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the close. The first third comes off there.
questions.simple: 3R is the fill plus three times the distance from the fill to the stop, which is 26.27.

questions.q: What does the post-gap high do to the first third?
choices: A cue to sell early; 3R is the rule
It replaces 3R as the first-third spot
It moves the first third out to 5R
Nothing; it is not part of the plan
questions.answer: A cue to sell early; 3R is the rule
questions.why: A cue to sell early. By our current default the first third is a third at 3R, and another third comes off at 5R, with the last third on the trail. The post-gap high can tell you to take the 3R third early. It does not change the thirds.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R is the rule. The post-gap high is a cue to take it early.

wrong.It replaces 3R as the first-third spot: By our current default the plan stays a third at 3R. The post-gap high does not replace it.
wrong.It moves the first third out to 5R: The second third is at 5R. The post-gap high does not push the first one out.
wrong.Nothing; it is not part of the plan: It is a cue. When it comes before 3R, you may take the first third early.

questions.simple: The post-gap high is only a cue to sell the first third early, while the rule stays a third at 3R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: Where does the stop go on a Gap Support buy?
choices: Just under the test day's low
Under the gap-fill for room
Exactly on the gap-up low
A fixed 2% under the gap low
questions.answer: Just under the test day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the test day's low. The stop is set from the test day's low, not from the gap-up low. It is not a fixed 1% to 3% cushion. Under the gap-fill spot the stop is a median 6% away. Only 12% are within 3%, and it wins less often per R.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the test day's low.

wrong.Under the gap-fill for room: That stop is a median 6% away.
wrong.Exactly on the gap-up low: The stop sits a few cents under the test day's low, not exactly on a low or a line.
wrong.A fixed 2% under the gap low: A fixed 1% to 3% cushion is not our stop.

questions.simple: The stop goes a few cents under the test day's low, not under the gap-fill spot and not a fixed cushion.

deeper.trap: Picking the wide stop for room. Under the gap-fill spot the stop is a median 6% away, and only 12% sit within 3%. The card also records that this stop wins less often per R.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The stop moves to breakeven at the first ___ by default.
questions.answer: trim
questions.why: Trim. The rulebook puts the move to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The Gap Support card sets it at the first trim by default.
questions.lesson_line: First trim, then the stop to breakeven.
questions.simple: Breakeven comes at the first trim by default, and the rulebook allows it anywhere from 2R to 5R.

questions.q: The last third trails a close under the 21-day for a fast mover or the 10-day for a steadier one.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. It is the other way round. Sell the last third on a close under the 10-day for a fast mover or the 21-day for a steadier one.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the last third under the 10- or 21-day.

questions.q: How far must price pull back before the test?
choices: At least 1 ATR under the post-gap high
At least 10% under the post-gap high
Any dip at all
Back to the prior close
questions.answer: At least 1 ATR under the post-gap high
questions.why: At least 1 ATR under the post-gap high. The close before the test sits at least 1 ATR under the post-gap high.
questions.lesson_line: A real pullback is at least one ATR deep.

wrong.At least 10% under the post-gap high: The measure is in ATRs, not a fixed percent.
wrong.Any dip at all: A shallow dip is not a pullback to the line.
wrong.Back to the prior close: Back to the prior close is the gap-fill spot; that kills the setup.

questions.q: Fill 15.96, stop 15.48. How far is the stop from the fill, in percent?
questions.why: 3.0. The fill minus the stop, divided by the fill. That is right at the 'about 3%' line. If the honest stop is more than about 3% away, size down or skip, and never pull it in. VIAV had these levels and ran to 25.4R.
questions.lesson_line: Stop distance is the fill minus the stop, over the fill.
questions.simple: Take the fill minus the stop, divide by the fill, and you get 3.0 percent, right at the 3 percent line.

reasons: computed key; the 'about 3%' line is marked settled on the card

questions.q: Buy the close?
questions.story: The test day undercut the gap-up low by 4% and ended the day 3% below it.
choices: Pass; the day did not hold the line
Buy the close; undercuts are fine
Buy half at the close, to be safe
Buy the close, stop at gap fill
questions.answer: Pass; the day did not hold the line
questions.why: No buy. The test day ended 3% under the gap-up low, so the line did not hold and there was no reclaim. A close under the gap-up low with no reclaim is a failed gap.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the line is not a hold.

wrong.Buy the close; undercuts are fine: An undercut alone can be fine. This day also ended under the line, and that close with no reclaim is a failed gap.
wrong.Buy half at the close, to be safe: Half size on a failed test is still a failed test.
wrong.Buy the close, stop at gap fill: Our stop is not under the gap-fill spot. That stop is a median 6% away.

questions.simple: Do not buy, because the day ended under the gap-up low, so the line did not hold.

reasons: tied to a held decision (D-094, the close allowance under the line)

questions.q: Buy the close?
questions.story: At 3:55 the stock sits on the gap-up low but is still making new lows for the day.
choices: No; it is still falling into the close
Yes; it is right on the line
Yes, with a tight stop
Yes; the gap is still open
questions.answer: No; it is still falling into the close
questions.why: No. A test day still falling into the close, with no hold and no reclaim, is not the setup.
questions.lesson_line: No hold and no reclaim means no buy.

wrong.Yes; it is right on the line: Sitting on the line is not enough; the day must hold and close back strong.
wrong.Yes, with a tight stop: A tight stop does not fix a day still falling.
wrong.Yes; the gap is still open: The gap being open is one test; the hold is another.

questions.q: What is the plan for the first third?
questions.story: You bought a test at 53.27 with the stop at 52.40. The post-gap high is 55.63, just under 3R.
choices: A third at 3R, 55.88; 55.63 is a cue
A third at the post-gap high, 55.63
Only at 5R; skip the first third
Hold the whole position and trail
questions.answer: A third at 3R, 55.88; 55.63 is a cue
questions.why: A third at 3R, 55.88. One R is the fill minus the stop, 53.27 minus 52.40, and three of those above the fill is 55.88. By our current default the rule is a third at 3R, another third at 5R, then the last third on the trail. The post-gap high at 55.63 sits just under 3R. It is a cue to take that third early, not a new rule.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R. The post-gap high is a cue to take it early.

wrong.A third at the post-gap high, 55.63: By our current default the rule stays a third at 3R. The post-gap high is a cue, not a new rule.
wrong.Only at 5R; skip the first third: The first third comes off at 3R. The 5R third is the second one.
wrong.Hold the whole position and trail: Only the last third rides the trail. The first third comes off at 3R.

questions.simple: Sell the first third at 3R, 55.88. The post-gap high, 55.63, is only a cue to take it early.

questions.q: Buy or pass?
questions.story: You planned to buy the test day's close at 50.00 but were away from your desk. The next morning the stock opens at 52.30.
choices: Pass; that is too far to chase
Buy, the hold is confirmed
Buy half size to cut risk
Buy with a wider stop
questions.answer: Pass; that is too far to chase
questions.why: Pass. 52.30 is more than 4% over the 50.00 buy point, and we never buy more than 4% above it. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Miss it rather than chase it. Four percent and done.

wrong.Buy, the hold is confirmed: A confirmed hold is not the question. The chase line is 4% above the buy point.
wrong.Buy half size to cut risk: The rule limits the price, not the size: no buy more than 4% over the buy point.
wrong.Buy with a wider stop: The stop goes where the chart puts it and never gets wider. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

questions.simple: Pass, because the open is more than 4% above your buy point, and we never chase past 4%.

deeper.trap: A confirmed hold feels like a reason to buy anyway. But the setup being right does not move the line. The limit is 4% over the buy point, and past it, chasing shrinks the size, not the risk.

questions.q: Buy the test?
questions.story: A clean test day closes back over the line on Wednesday. The company reports Thursday after the close.
choices: No; a report is within 3 days
Yes; the test day is clean
Yes, but at half size only
Yes, and hold through the report
questions.answer: No; a report is within 3 days
questions.why: No. We take no new buy in the 3 days before an earnings report. The report comes after Thursday's close, so a Wednesday buy is inside that window. Holding through a report needs a trade already up 5R, and this would be a new buy.
questions.lesson_line: A report within 3 days means no new buy.

wrong.Yes; the test day is clean: A clean chart does not remove the report risk.
wrong.Yes, but at half size only: Half size is still a new buy in the report window.
wrong.Yes, and hold through the report: Holding through a report needs a trade already up 5R, not a new position.

questions.simple: Do not buy, because the report is within 3 days and we take no new buy that close to earnings.

questions.q: How do you handle this stop?
questions.story: The test day's low puts your stop 5% under the fill. A friend says to use 1.5% under the fill instead, so you can buy more shares.
choices: Buy fewer shares to fit the 5% stop
Pull the stop in to 1.5% under the fill
Buy the usual share count anyway
Put the stop at the gap-fill spot
questions.answer: Buy fewer shares to fit the 5% stop
questions.why: Buy fewer shares. The stop goes a few cents under the test day's low, and the size comes from that stop. When the stop is more than about 3% away, size down or skip. Never pull the stop in.
questions.lesson_line: If the honest stop does not fit, size down or skip.

wrong.Put the stop at the gap-fill spot: The gap-fill spot sits below the line, so a stop there is even wider. It does not fit the size.
wrong.Pull the stop in to 1.5% under the fill: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is the mistake, not the plan.
wrong.Buy the usual share count anyway: The usual count on a 5% stop risks more than the plan allows. The size comes from the stop.

questions.simple: Buy fewer shares, because the stop stays under the test day's low and is never pulled in.

reasons: rests on the owner's stop-first and sizing rules (A3, A5)
wrong note on the gap-fill spot reworded to the cited median

questions.q: Ten days in, what is the move?
questions.story: You bought a Gap Support test. Ten trading days later it sits at 0.3R, never near 3R and never near the stop.
choices: Sell; under 1R at 10 trading days
Hold; the stop has not been hit
Sell half now and hold the rest
Move the stop to breakeven and wait
questions.answer: Sell; under 1R at 10 trading days
questions.why: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, which frees the money. At 0.3R after ten days this trade is under 1R, so the time stop applies. The stop was never hit, and the trade is not working.
questions.lesson_line: A slow trade under 1R gets sold on day ten.

wrong.Hold; the stop has not been hit: The time stop exists for exactly this trade.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven and wait: The stop goes to breakeven at the first trim by default, not as a way to keep waiting.
wrong.Sell half now and hold the rest: The time stop sells the trade. It does not trim it.

questions.simple: Sell it, because a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days hits the time stop, even though the stop was never touched.

reasons: rests on the owner's time-stop rule (C33)

questions.q: What does the Red reading call for?
questions.story: The market reading is Red. A leader's test day holds the gap-up low, closes in the upper half, and the 50-day is rising.
choices: Mostly cash and shorts
Full risk, up to 10 positions
Smaller and fewer positions
Only A+ setups, nothing lower
questions.answer: Mostly cash and shorts
questions.why: Mostly cash and shorts. In a Red market we are mostly in cash and short. Green is full risk, Yellow is smaller and fewer, and Orange is A+ only.
questions.lesson_line: Red market: mostly cash and shorts.

wrong.Full risk, up to 10 positions: Full risk is the Green reading.
wrong.Smaller and fewer positions: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Red means mostly cash and shorts.
wrong.Only A+ setups, nothing lower: Only A+ setups is the Orange reading. Red means mostly cash and shorts.

questions.simple: Mostly cash and shorts. That is what a Red reading means.

reasons: rests on the owner's market-reading rule (A10, F65)

questions.q: Gap Support or PEG?
questions.story: A stock gapped 9% on earnings this morning and is holding near the high of the day. You are deciding which setup owns today's buy.
choices: A PEG; the gap day is not Gap Support
Gap Support; the gap is holding
Gap Support; today's low is the line
Neither; there is no setup on a gap day
questions.answer: A PEG; the gap day is not Gap Support
questions.why: A PEG. The gap day itself is a PEG, never Gap Support. A PEG is bought on the gap day or its first pause, with the gap-day low as the outer stop. Gap Support waits for price to come back to the gap-up day's low and defend it.
questions.lesson_line: Count the days since the gap. Day zero is a PEG.

wrong.Gap Support; the gap is holding: Holding today is the PEG day; Gap Support is a later test.
wrong.Gap Support; today's low is the line: Today's low is not yet a line that has been tested and defended.
wrong.Neither; there is no setup on a gap day: A PEG is bought on the gap day or its first pause.

questions.simple: A PEG. The gap day is a PEG, and Gap Support is the later test when price returns to the gap-up low.

questions.q: Gap Support or HVE line?
questions.story: Two marked lines sit near price. One is the low of the gap-up day. The other is the close of a record-volume day. You are asking which line this lesson defends.
choices: The gap-up day's low must hold
The record day's close must hold
Either one; they are the same
Neither; the 50-day decides
questions.answer: The gap-up day's low must hold
questions.why: The gap-up day's low must hold. Gap Support's line is the gap-up day's low, and the gap must still be open. The High Volume Edge's line is the record-volume day's close, and price may trade under that close without harm. They are different setups with different lines.
questions.lesson_line: Gap Support defends a low. The HVE defends a close.

wrong.The record day's close must hold: That is the HVE's line, and price may trade under it without harm.
wrong.Either one; they are the same: They are different setups with different lines.
wrong.Neither; the 50-day decides: The 50-day is a filter, not the line.

questions.simple: The gap-up day's low. Gap Support defends that low while the gap is open, but the High Volume Edge defends a record-volume close.

questions.q: What kind of gap is this?
questions.story: A stock gapped down off its highs. Weeks later price is rallying back up toward the gap.
choices: A bear gap; its high must cap price
Gap Support; the gap will act as support
Gap Support; buy as it fills the gap
A buyable gap-up; price is rallying
questions.answer: A bear gap; its high must cap price
questions.why: A bear gap, not Gap Support. A bear gap is a gap down off the highs, and its high must cap price. Gap Support is a gap up above a flat or rising 50-day whose low holds. On our card a bear gap is never a long.
questions.lesson_line: A gap down is a bear gap, not Gap Support.

wrong.Gap Support; the gap will act as support: A gap down is not support for a long. Gap Support is a gap up.
wrong.Gap Support; buy as it fills the gap: Buying a rally into a gap down is the opposite of this setup.
wrong.A buyable gap-up; price is rallying: This gap went down, so it is not a gap-up.

questions.simple: A bear gap, not Gap Support. A gap down off the highs is the opposite of this setup.

questions.q: Gap Support or Undercut and Rally?
questions.story: The stock gapped up months ago. Now price undercuts the lowest low of a base from five weeks ago and closes back over it two days later. The gap-up day's low is far below.
choices: Undercut and Rally; a swing low
Gap Support; it gapped up
A PEG; reclaimed a swing low
Neither; a reclaim is one day
questions.answer: Undercut and Rally; a swing low
questions.why: An Undercut and Rally. On our card a U&R reclaims a prominent prior swing low on the daily chart within 3 sessions. Here price undercut the low of a base and closed back over it two days later. Gap Support's undercut is of a gap-up day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Name the low that was undercut. A swing low is a U&R.

wrong.Gap Support; it gapped up: Gap Support's undercut is of the gap-up day's low. This undercut is of a base low.
wrong.A PEG; reclaimed a swing low: A PEG is the gap day itself or its first pause. This is a later reclaim of a swing low.
wrong.Neither; a reclaim is one day: Our card lets a reclaim take up to 3 sessions, so two days fits.

questions.simple: An Undercut and Rally. It undercut a swing low of a base, not a gap-up day's low.

questions.q: Which test is stronger?
questions.story: Two tests of two gaps. One holds the gap-up low to the tick and closes on a hammer. The other trades down to the prior day's high and reclaims the line by the close.
choices: First stronger; a hold beats a fill
Second stronger; it tested harder
Both equal; both closed over the line
Neither is a valid Gap Support test
questions.answer: First stronger; a hold beats a fill
questions.why: The first test is stronger. Our card ranks a hold first, then a slight breach, then a fill to the gap-fill spot that reclaims the line. A fill that reclaims is allowed, but it ranks last.
questions.lesson_line: Held beats a slight breach, and a fill that reclaims ranks last.

wrong.Second stronger; it tested harder: A deeper fill is weaker, not stronger.
wrong.Both equal; both closed over the line: Both ended well, but the card ranks a hold above a fill that reclaims.
wrong.Neither is a valid Gap Support test: A fill that reclaims the line is allowed. It just ranks below a hold.

questions.simple: The first test is stronger. It held the gap-up low, and a fill that only reclaims the line ranks last.

reasons: teaches the card's ranking of tests, not a fixed grade (E50 keeps grading a judgment call)

questions.q: Which grades higher, and why?
questions.story: Same clean test day on two stocks. One gapped 10% and the other gapped 35%.
choices: The 10% gap; a gap over 30% is lower
The 35% gap; bigger gaps are stronger
Neither; both are banned
The same; the test day decides
questions.answer: The 10% gap; a gap over 30% is lower
questions.why: The 10% gap. A gap over 30% is a lower grade, not a ban. Wagner warns that an opening gap of more than 30% could lead to a few months of chop. On the same clean test day, the smaller gap grades higher.
questions.lesson_line: A gap over 30% grades lower, but it is not banned.

wrong.The 35% gap; bigger gaps are stronger: A very large gap tends to chop; it grades lower.
wrong.Neither; both are banned: A gap over 30% is a lower grade, not a ban.
wrong.The same; the test day decides: The gap size is part of the grade, even on a clean test.

questions.simple: The 10% gap grades higher, because a gap over 30% grades lower, though it is not banned.

deeper.trap: Reading 'lower grade' as 'banned'. The card lowers the grade over 30% and does not forbid it. Wagner's warning is about a few months of chop rather than quick follow-through, not about a failed trade.

reasons: one web source (Wagner), quote checked on the page

questions.q: Grade each close.
questions.story: Two test days hold the gap-up low. One closes near its high on a hammer with a long lower wick. The other closes at 60% of its range.
choices: First an A+ cue; second is plain
Both the same; both held the line
Second stronger; 60% is a safer close
Both A+; any hold is good enough
questions.answer: First an A+ cue; second is plain
questions.why: First an A+ cue, second a plain test. The A+ cue has two parts. The gap-up low holds, and the day closes back above it near its high on a lower wick or hammer. A close at 60% of the range is in the upper half, so it holds the line. It is not near the high, so it earns no A+ cue.
questions.lesson_line: A hammer close near the high is A+. Upper half just holds.

wrong.Both the same; both held the line: Both held, but only the first closed near its high on a hammer, which is the A+ cue.
wrong.Both A+; any hold is good enough: Only a close near the high with a lower wick or hammer is the A+ cue. A close at 60% just holds.
wrong.Second stronger; 60% is a safer close: A hammer close near the high is the stronger look. A 60% close just holds.

questions.simple: A close near the high on a hammer is an A+ cue. A close at 60% of the range just holds the line.

deeper.trap: Do not mistake the gate for the grade. A close in the upper half only passes the test. Near the high with a lower wick or hammer is the A+ cue. A close in the lower part of the range is a B- cue.

reasons: the card's close-position rows overlap (upper-half gate against a lower-part B- cue)

questions.q: Which pullback do traders like best?
questions.story: Two stocks pull back to the line. One drifts down on lighter volume. The other falls on heavy-volume selling.
choices: The quiet one on lighter volume
The heavy-volume one; it is a flush
Neither; volume does not matter
Both the same; the line decides
questions.answer: The quiet one on lighter volume
questions.why: The quiet one on lighter volume. Heavy-volume selling into the line is a warning, not a rule.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet pullbacks are the good ones.

wrong.The heavy-volume one; it is a flush: Heavy-volume selling into the line is a warning.
wrong.Neither; volume does not matter: Volume is a cue here, not noise.
wrong.Both the same; the line decides: The line matters, and so does how price gets there.

questions.q: Account 50,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 53.27, stop 52.40. How many shares does the risk allow?
questions.why: 287 shares. The risk is 0.5% of 50,000. Divide that by the fill minus the stop, 53.27 minus 52.40, and round down. The stop sets the size. The position cap is a second limit; this question asks for the risk-based size.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: Divide the 0.5% risk on 50,000 by the distance from fill to stop, and round down to get 287 shares.

questions.q: Where does the stop go?
questions.story: Midday on the test day, price undercuts the gap-up low and reclaims it on the 30-minute chart. You want to buy the reclaim.
choices: Just under the day's low so far
At the gap-fill for more room
Exactly on the gap-up low
A fixed 2% under the reclaim
questions.answer: Just under the day's low so far
questions.why: A few cents under the test day's low so far. The intraday version is an undercut and reclaim of the gap-up low, a red to green, or an hourly higher low. It uses the same stop. The stop is not on the line, not at the gap-fill spot and not a fixed percent.
questions.lesson_line: Same stop on the intraday version.

wrong.At the gap-fill for more room: The gap-fill spot is a median 6% away, far from the entry.
wrong.Exactly on the gap-up low: The stop sits a few cents under a low, not on the line.
wrong.A fixed 2% under the reclaim: The stop comes from a real low, not a fixed percent.

questions.simple: Just under the day's low so far, by a few cents. The intraday version uses the same stop as the daily one.

reasons: owner's Sunday Scans quote on one stock

questions.q: Kacher and Morales allow a 1-2% undercut, so our stop is a fixed 1-3% under the gap-up low.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Kacher and Morales say a 1-2% undercut can be permitted in some cases. That is about how far price may dip. Our stop is a few cents under the test day's low, not a fixed 1% to 3% cushion under the gap-up low.
questions.lesson_line: A real low sets the stop, not a fixed cushion.
questions.simple: False. Kacher and Morales allow a 1 to 2% undercut in some cases, but our stop is a few cents under the test day's low.

reasons: one web quote, checked on the page

questions.q: The gap day can close back inside the prior day's range and still count.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The gap day closes above the prior day's high. It must also be a true gap, where the whole day trades above that high. A close back inside the prior range fails the test, so the setup never starts.
questions.lesson_line: The gap day must close above the prior day's high.
questions.simple: False. The gap day must close above the prior day's high, so a close back inside the prior range fails that test.

questions.q: The post-gap high is 24.00. The close before the test is 22.20. The 14-day ATR is 0.90. How many ATRs is the pullback?
questions.why: 2.0 ATR. Take the post-gap high minus the close before the test, then divide by the ATR. The pullback has to be at least 1 ATR under the post-gap high, so 2.0 clears it.
questions.lesson_line: Pullback depth is measured in ATRs.
questions.simple: Divide the drop from the post-gap high to the close before the test by the ATR. That gives 2.0, above the 1 ATR minimum.

reasons: computed key; a proposed card criterion

questions.q: Take the test?
questions.story: A test day holds the gap-up low and closes in the upper half. The stock's RS rating is 52 and its group is one of the weakest.
choices: No; it is a laggard, not a leader
No; it needs a deeper undercut
Yes; the test holds, closes high
Yes, but at half the usual size
questions.answer: No; it is a laggard, not a leader
questions.why: No. We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. At 52, in one of the weakest groups, this stock is a laggard, and a clean test does not change that.
questions.lesson_line: A leader first: RS 80 or more, in a strong group.

wrong.No; it needs a deeper undercut: No undercut is required. The problem here is leadership.
wrong.Yes; the test holds, closes high: A clean chart on a laggard is not our setup.
wrong.Yes, but at half the usual size: Half size does not turn a laggard into a leader.

questions.simple: No. Gap Support wants a leader, and an RS rating of 52 in one of the weakest groups is not one.

reasons: rests on the owner's leader rule (C31)

questions.q: Buy the close?
questions.story: A test day holds the line and closes strong, but the close is 12% above the 10-day average.
choices: No; more than 10% over the 10-day
No; the close must sit under the 10-day
Yes; the test day looks textbook
Yes, but only at half the usual size
questions.answer: No; more than 10% over the 10-day
questions.why: No. We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average. At 12% over, the stock is too stretched to buy, however textbook the test looks. At 10% or less it passes this check.
questions.lesson_line: Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day.

wrong.No; the close must sit under the 10-day: Our stretch rule is about being more than 10% above the 10-day, not about sitting under it.
wrong.Yes; the test day looks textbook: A textbook chart still has to pass the stretch rule.
wrong.Yes, but only at half the usual size: Half size does not fix a stretched entry.

questions.simple: No. We skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average, and 12% is over that line.

reasons: rests on the owner's stretch rule (C29)
the question says buy the close, which waits on D-003

questions.q: Do you buy?
questions.story: A test day holds the gap-up low and closes in the upper half, but the close is under the 200-day.
choices: No; the test closed under the 200-day
Yes; the line held
Yes, at half size
Yes; the 50-day is rising
questions.answer: No; the test closed under the 200-day
questions.why: No. A test day that closes under the 200-day is off. No longs below the 200-day simple moving average.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, no buy.

wrong.Yes; the line held: Holding the line is not enough under the 200-day.
wrong.Yes, at half size: Half size does not fix a 200-day failure.
wrong.Yes; the 50-day is rising: A rising 50-day does not lift a close over the 200-day.

questions.q: What was that loss?
questions.story: AVGO. A 16.2% earnings gap on 4.3x volume. Thirteen sessions later the test day holds near perfectly, and you buy the close with the stop a few cents under the test day's low. The stop trades without any gain.
choices: A planned loss; a clean test can lose
A sign the setup no longer works
A mistake; you should have held
A broken rule; stop too tight
questions.answer: A planned loss; a clean test can lose
questions.why: A planned loss; a clean test can still lose. In the AVGO case the hold was near perfect, with the low 0.7% above the line. The stop still traded without any gain. The stop is the exit, a few cents under the test day's low, so taking it is the plan working.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the exit, even on a clean test.

wrong.A sign the setup no longer works: One loss does not show that. AVGO held near perfectly and still lost. A clean test can lose.
wrong.A mistake; you should have held: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never wider.
wrong.A broken rule; stop too tight: The stop sat a few cents under the test day's low, as the rules say.

questions.simple: A planned loss. A near perfect test can still lose, and the stop is the exit, so taking it is the system working.

deeper.trap: Calling the loss a mistake because the chart was clean. This test closed at 88% of its range with 1.7% risk, and the stop still traded without any gain. Judge the trade by whether the rules were followed, not by one result.

reasons: rests on the owner's stop rule (A4)
example read from our own bars, not yet reviewed
story says buy the close, D-003

questions.q: What does the second close tell you?
questions.story: AEHR. The test day closes on the line with a hammer. The stop trades the next session. Two sessions later the stock closes under the gap-fill spot.
choices: The gap filled; the setup is dead
The line held; buy again
A fresh Gap Support; buy the close
A bounce is due; wait
questions.answer: The gap filled; the setup is dead
questions.why: The gap filled; the setup is dead. A close at or under the gap-fill spot, the prior day's high, means the gap filled. The hammer close on the line was fine, and the stop traded the next session. The later close under the spot ended any new buy.
questions.lesson_line: A close at the gap-fill spot ends it for good.

wrong.The line held; buy again: A close at the gap-fill spot means the line failed.
wrong.A fresh Gap Support; buy the close: A close under the gap-fill spot is a dead gap, not a fresh one.
wrong.A bounce is due; wait: Waiting for a bounce on a dead gap is hope.

questions.simple: The gap filled, so the setup is dead. A close under the gap-fill spot ends it, even after a hammer on the line.

deeper.trap: Buying again because the first stop-out felt unlucky. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Here the gap filled on a close two sessions later, and the stock halved by 10-30.

reasons: example read from our own bars, not yet reviewed

questions.q: What was the missing filter?
questions.story: AMD, 2020. An 11.7% gap on 2.2x volume. Thirty-five sessions later the test closes at 97% of its range. The stop trades with no gain. The broad market was pulling back.
choices: The market reading
The gap size
The test-day close
The stop distance
questions.answer: The market reading
questions.why: The market reading. The test closed at 97% of its range, yet the broad market was in a pullback. The scan ignores the market reading; the rulebook does not.
questions.lesson_line: A great test in a weak market is still a weak trade.

wrong.The gap size: An 11.7% gap is not the problem.
wrong.The stop distance: The stop sat under the test day's low.

questions.q: Take it or pass?
questions.story: DE, 2026. A 6.8% gap on 4.4x volume. Four sessions later the test closes at 0.01 of its range, 0.8% under the line.
choices: Pass; still falling into the close
Take it; it is only 0.8% under
Take it; the gap is open
Take it; the volume was huge
questions.answer: Pass; still falling into the close
questions.why: Pass. The test closed at 0.01 of its range, 0.8% under the line. A day still falling into the close, with no hold and no reclaim, is not the setup.
questions.lesson_line: A test that closes at its low is not a hold.

wrong.Take it; it is only 0.8% under: A close at the low is not a hold, however small the miss.
wrong.Take it; the gap is open: An open gap is one test; the hold is another.
wrong.Take it; the volume was huge: Volume on the gap day does not rescue a weak test.

questions.q: Take it or pass?
questions.story: DOCU, 2025. A 9.1% gap on 5.4x volume closed 2.6% under a falling 50-day. Eleven sessions later the test looks fine.
choices: Pass; the gap is in a downtrend
Pass; the test came too long after
Take it; the test day looks clean
Take it; 5.4x volume is huge
questions.answer: Pass; the gap is in a downtrend
questions.why: Pass. We take no downtrend gaps: the gap day must close above a flat or rising 50-day. DOCU closed 2.6% under a falling 50-day. The test 11 sessions later looked fine, but it was a bounce in a downtrend, 0.0R if taken.
questions.lesson_line: A clean test in a downtrend is still a bounce.

wrong.Take it; the test day looks clean: A clean test does not cancel the downtrend.
wrong.Take it; 5.4x volume is huge: Heavy volume does not turn a downtrend gap into a leader.
wrong.Pass; the test came too long after: The wait is not the problem. A long drift back to the line is not a minus by itself.

questions.simple: Pass. The gap day closed under a falling 50-day, so the test was a bounce in a downtrend, however fine it looked.

deeper.trap: Judging the gap by size and volume alone. A 9.1% gap on 5.4x volume sounds strong, but the trend check still applies. Here the 50-day was 3.2% lower than 10 sessions earlier, so the gap was a downtrend gap.

reasons: example read from our own bars, not yet reviewed

questions.q: Take it or pass?
questions.story: EVR, 2019. An 11.3% gap on 4.1x volume above a rising 50-day. Six sessions later the test closes 6.9% under the 200-day.
choices: Pass; it closed under the 200-day
Pass; the 50-day is not rising enough
Take it; the gap is huge on volume
Take it, but at half the usual size
questions.answer: Pass; it closed under the 200-day
questions.why: Pass. The test closed 6.9% under the 200-day. The gap came on 4.1x volume above a rising 50-day. Still, we take no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the 200-day means pass, however good the rest looks.

wrong.Take it; the gap is huge on volume: Gap size does not change the 200-day rule.
wrong.Pass; the 50-day is not rising enough: The 50-day was rising. The problem is the 200-day.
wrong.Take it, but at half the usual size: Half size does not fix a 200-day failure.

questions.simple: Pass. The test closed 6.9% under the 200-day, and we take no longs below the 200-day.

deeper.trap: Letting a strong gap overrule the 200-day. An 11.3% gap on 4.1x volume above a rising 50-day looks strong. The test day still closed under the 200-day, and the rule is checked on the test day's close.

reasons: example read from our own bars

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought at 20.00 with the stop at 19.40. A report gaps it down to 18.70, and the first 30-minute bar's low is 18.50.
choices: Get out; the loss is past 2R
Set the stop at 18.50, wait
Stop at 19.40; it'll bounce
Add at 18.50 to lower cost
questions.answer: Get out; the loss is past 2R
questions.why: Get out. On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop. With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. Here the low, 18.50, is more than 2R under the 20.00 fill, where one R is the distance from 20.00 to 19.40.
questions.lesson_line: Past 2R in the first half hour, get out.

wrong.Set the stop at 18.50, wait: The first 30-minute low is the new stop only while the loss is within 2R. Past 2R, you get out.
wrong.Stop at 19.40; it'll bounce: The gap went through that stop. The rule sets a new one, or sends you out, and does not wait for a bounce.
wrong.Add at 18.50 to lower cost: Adding breaks one buy, one price, one stop.

questions.simple: Get out, because the gap took the loss past 2R in the first half hour.

deeper.trap: Do not read the 30-minute rule as wait for the low. The low only becomes the new stop when the loss is within 2R. Past 2R it is a ceiling, and you are out. A test near earnings season can gap, so this can happen on a clean setup.

questions.q: By our plan, where does the first third go?
questions.story: LLY, 2021. A news gap. The test is bought at 231.13 with the stop at 228.43. The post-gap high is 239.37.
choices: A third at 3R, at 239.23
A third at 239.37
A third at 5R, not yet
A third on a 240 close
questions.answer: A third at 3R, at 239.23
questions.why: A third at 3R, 239.23. One R is the fill minus the stop, 231.13 minus 228.43. Three of those above the fill is 239.23. The post-gap high, 239.37, sits above 3R, so it comes second and the third stays at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: The first third comes off at 3R.

wrong.A third at 239.37: The first third comes off at 3R, and 239.23 comes before 239.37.
wrong.A third at 5R, not yet: The first third comes off before 5R. The 5R third is the second one.
wrong.A third on a 240 close: There is no rule to wait for 240.

questions.simple: Sell the first third at 3R, 239.23. The post-gap high, 239.37, is above 3R, so it comes second.

deeper.trap: The two levels sit close together, so it is easy to pick the high. The plan is a third at 3R, and 3R is reached first.

questions.q: May you take it?
questions.story: You were stopped out of the same gap-up low three times this week. On Friday it tests the line again and closes strong.
choices: No; the weekly limit is reached
Yes; new trigger, new trade
No; never rebuy after a stop
Yes, with a wider stop
questions.answer: No; the weekly limit is reached
questions.why: No. We allow at most 3 tries a week and 6 a month on the same line. You were stopped out three times this week, so the weekly tries are used. After a stop-out, a new trigger makes a new trade, but only inside that cap.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week on one line, then stop.

wrong.Yes; new trigger, new trade: A new trigger is a new trade, but the tries per week are capped at 3.
wrong.No; never rebuy after a stop: After a stop-out we may buy again on a new trigger. Here the weekly cap is what says no.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop: The stop goes a few cents under the test day's low. If it does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

questions.simple: No, because we allow at most 3 tries a week on one line and you have used all of them.

deeper.trap: A new trigger after a stop-out is a new trade with its own stop and every rule, so it feels allowed. But the cap still counts: 3 tries a week and 6 a month on the same line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E56, B21)

questions.q: For Gap Support, a gap that price never comes back to is no setup. The setup is the later test.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. For Gap Support, a gap that is never revisited is no setup. The gap day itself is a PEG. The setup is the later test, when price comes back to the gap-up day's low and defends it.
questions.lesson_line: No test, no setup.
questions.simple: True. For Gap Support, a gap that price never comes back to is no setup, because the setup is the later test.

deeper.trap: Treating every gap as a Gap Support candidate. The gap day belongs to the PEG. A Gap Support buy exists only after price returns to the line and the test day passes the checks.

questions.q: Which order ranks the tests, best to worst?
choices: Held, slight breach, fill that reclaims
Fill that reclaims, held, slight breach
Slight breach, held, fill that reclaims
All three grade the same
questions.answer: Held, slight breach, fill that reclaims
questions.why: Held, slight breach, fill that reclaims. A fill that reclaims the gap-up low is allowed but graded B- at best.
questions.lesson_line: Held, then a slight breach, then a fill that reclaims.

wrong.Fill that reclaims, held, slight breach: A fill that reclaims is the weakest of the three, not the best.
wrong.Slight breach, held, fill that reclaims: Holding to the tick ranks above a slight breach.
wrong.All three grade the same: The ranking is held first, and the fill is the lesser grade.

questions.q: Which test is the weaker one?
questions.story: Test A comes after six weeks of chop sitting on the line. Test B comes seven weeks after the gap, a clean 15% slide straight back to the line.
choices: A; weeks of chop on the line is B-
B; seven weeks is too late to buy
Both the same; time does not matter
B; a 15% slide back is a failure
questions.answer: A; weeks of chop on the line is B-
questions.why: A. Weeks of chop sitting on the line before the test is a B- cue on our card. A long drift back to the line is not a minus by itself. AXON's test came 35 sessions after the gap. A 15% slide from the post-gap high stopped on the gap-up low with a hammer.
questions.lesson_line: Chop on the line is a B- cue. A long drift is not.

wrong.B; seven weeks is too late to buy: A long drift back to the line is not a minus by itself.
wrong.Both the same; time does not matter: Time alone is not a minus, but the weeks of chop on the line in test A are a B- cue.
wrong.B; a 15% slide back is a failure: A slide that stops on the line is the pullback.

questions.simple: Test A is weaker. Weeks of chop on the line is a B- cue, but a long drift back is not a minus.

deeper.trap: Treating time as the grade. AXON's test came 35 sessions after the gap, 6.4 ATR off the 193.85 high, and it still stopped on the gap-up low with a hammer. What lowers the grade is chop on the line, not the weeks it took to get there.

reasons: teaches a card grade while E50 calls grading a judgment call
the card's timing window is held (D-095)
example read from our own bars

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought the test day's close. A friend says you can watch the stop by hand since you are at your screen all day.
choices: Place the stop order with the broker now
Watch it by hand today
Use a mental stop under the low
Set it tomorrow after the open
questions.answer: Place the stop order with the broker now
questions.why: Place the stop order with the broker now. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. It only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: A real stop order, placed with the buy.

wrong.Watch it by hand today: A stop in your head is not a stop; screens fail and moods change.
wrong.Use a mental stop under the low: A mental stop is the same mistake.
wrong.Set it tomorrow after the open: The risk starts at the buy; so does the stop order.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the test day is the last bar. Judging the test day alone, buy the close or pass?
choices: Take it; closed back over the line
Pass; the gap has already filled
Pass; it closed in the lower half
Pass; it closed under the gap-up low
questions.answer: Take it; closed back over the line
questions.why: Take it. The low dipped 0.3% under the 27.00 gap-up low, but the day closed at 27.15, back over the line. That close is 62% of its range, in the upper half. The scan bought 27.15 with the stop at 26.89.
questions.lesson_line: A hold at the line with a strong close is the setup.

wrong.Pass; the gap has already filled: The gap was still open. No close had sat at or under the prior day's high since the gap day.
wrong.Pass; it closed in the lower half: The close was at 62% of its range, in the upper half.
wrong.Pass; it closed under the gap-up low: It dipped under the line but closed back over it.

questions.simple: Take it. The low dipped 0.3% under the gap-up low, but the day closed back over it, in the upper half.

deeper.trap: A dip under the line is not a failed test. A close under the line with no reclaim is. So is a day still falling into the close.

reasons: tied to a held decision (D-003, buy the close)
example numbers are from our own bars and not yet owner-reviewed

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the test day is the last bar. Did it hold the line and close back strong? Buy the close or pass.
choices: Pass; it closed right at its low
Pass; it needs a deeper undercut first
Take it; it held the line today
Take it; a small undercut is fine
questions.answer: Pass; it closed right at its low
questions.why: Pass. The test closed at 0.01 of its range, 0.8% under the line, still falling into the close. A test with no hold and no reclaim is not the setup.
questions.lesson_line: A test that closes at its low is not a hold.

wrong.Take it; it held the line today: It closed under the line, not on it.
wrong.Pass; it needs a deeper undercut first: No undercut is required. This day failed because it closed at its low.
wrong.Take it; a small undercut is fine: This day had no hold and no reclaim, so it is not a slight breach.

questions.simple: Pass. The test day closed at the bottom of its range, 0.8% under the line, so it did not hold.

deeper.trap: Waving through a near miss. The card ranks tests as held, then a slight breach, then a fill that reclaims the line. This day was none of those: no hold and no reclaim, and it closed at 0.01 of its range.

questions.q: Which grade do these cues point to?
questions.story: A leader, RS 85, in a strong group, with growing sales and earnings. It gapped 10% on 4x volume. Eight sessions later a quiet pullback tags the line to the tick and closes near its high on a hammer. The stop is 2.1% away in a Green market.
choices: A+; all the cues line up
A; the gap is only 10%
B-; the test came too late
B-; the stop is too wide
questions.answer: A+; all the cues line up
questions.why: A+. Every cue shows, though grading stays a judgment. It is a leader (RS 85, strong group) with growing sales and earnings. The pullback is quiet on lighter volume. The line held to the tick, with a hammer close near the high. The risk is 2.1%, under 3%, in a Green market.
questions.lesson_line: When every cue lines up, it is an A+.

wrong.A; the gap is only 10%: A gap over 30% is the size flag. A 10% gap is no minus.
wrong.B-; the test came too late: A long drift back to the line is not a minus by itself, and this one took only eight sessions.
wrong.B-; the stop is too wide: The A+ cue is risk under 3%, and 2.1% is inside it.

questions.simple: A+, because the stock is a leader, the pullback is quiet, the line held to the tick and the risk is tight.

deeper.trap: Inventing minuses. A gap of 10% is not a flag, since a gap over 30% is the lower-grade flag. A long drift is not a minus, and this took only eight sessions. A hold to the tick is an A+ cue, not a flaw.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D38 grading)

questions.q: Why trade it at all?
questions.story: Bulkowski found that gaps in an uptrend show underlying support only 20% of the time in a bull market. A member asks why we trade Gap Support at all.
choices: Leaders, the right line, a tight stop
Gaps always fill, so fade every one
Volume on the gap day guarantees support
Ignore Bulkowski; he is wrong
questions.answer: Leaders, the right line, a tight stop
questions.why: Pick leaders, the right line and the market, and keep a tight stop. Bulkowski found gaps in an uptrend show support only 20% of the time, and in our scan 28.9% reached 3R. The edge is the stock, the level and the market, with small stops, not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: No guarantees: leader, line, market, and a tight stop.

wrong.Gaps always fill, so fade every one: Our rule is that buyable gaps do not fill, and we do not fade them.
wrong.Ignore Bulkowski; he is wrong: His count is a fair warning, not an error to ignore.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: DKS, 2021. You bought the test and the stop traded the next session on a 2.4% undercut that closed back on the line. Weeks later the stock has run far higher.
choices: Nothing; wait for a new trigger
Buy now; the reclaim was a new trigger
Rebuy now at double size to catch up
Widen your stops on the next buy
questions.answer: Nothing; wait for a new trigger
questions.why: Nothing now. The stop is the exit, and a re-entry needs a new trigger. The stop traded on a 2.4% undercut that closed back on the line, and the stock then ran to 147.39. Seeing that afterward does not change what the rule said at the time.
questions.lesson_line: A stop that was right by the rules stays right.

wrong.Widen your stops on the next buy: The stop goes a few cents under the test day's low. If it does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
wrong.Rebuy now at double size to catch up: A re-entry needs a new trigger, and the size comes from the risk percent and the stop, not from catching up.
wrong.Buy now; the reclaim was a new trigger: The reclaim was weeks ago. The stock is far above the buy point now, and we never buy more than 4% above it.

questions.simple: Do nothing now. The stop was the exit, and a new buy needs a new trigger, even though the stock ran.

deeper.trap: A stop-out that reverses feels like proof the stop was wrong. Here a 2.4% undercut closed back on the line and the stock ran to 147.39, yet the stop is the exit. A re-entry is a new trade with its own stop and every rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B21)

questions.q: Which stock passes our price and dollars-traded rule?
choices: $12 stock, $24M traded a day
$8 stock, $40M traded a day
$35 stock, $15M a day
$11 stock, $19M a day
questions.answer: $12 stock, $24M traded a day
questions.why: The $12 stock. Our rule is a price of $10 or more and at least $20 million traded a day. The $8 stock fails on price. The $35 stock at $15M and the $11 stock at $19M fail on dollars traded.
questions.lesson_line: Ten dollars and twenty million. Both tests, every time.

wrong.$8 stock, $40M traded a day: A price under $10 fails, whatever the volume.
wrong.$35 stock, $15M a day: Under $20 million a day fails, whatever the price.
wrong.$11 stock, $19M a day: Just under $20 million a day still fails the rule.

questions.story: Four stocks hold their gap-up lows today and close strong. You check the price and the dollars traded each day.
questions.simple: The $12 stock with $24M a day. Our rule needs a price of $10 or more and at least $20 million traded a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's price and dollars-traded rule (B23)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Gap Support needs $10 or more a share and $___ million traded a day.
questions.why: 20. Gap Support needs a price of $10 or more a share and $20 million or more traded a day. Both tests must pass.
questions.lesson_line: Ten dollars a share, twenty million a day.
questions.simple: 20. Gap Support needs a price of $10 or more and at least $20 million traded a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's price and volume rule (B23)

questions.q: The stock trades 600,000 shares a day on average. The most shares we may own?
questions.why: 6,000 shares. One percent of 600,000 is 6,000. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume is the ceiling.
questions.simple: Take 1 percent of the 600,000 shares a day, which gives 6,000 shares.

questions.q: Even on a clean Gap Support, we cap our position at 1% of the stock's average daily volume.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, however clean the setup. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Clean setup or not, one percent of the daily volume is the limit.
questions.simple: True. We never own more than 1 percent of a stock's average daily volume, even on a clean setup.

questions.q: Which do you prefer?
choices: The grower; the charts are equal
The flat-sales stock; it is safer
Neither; fundamentals are not a factor
The grower; the chart no longer matters
questions.answer: The grower; the charts are equal
questions.why: The grower. We prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings, but the chart comes first. Here the charts are equal, so growth is the preference that decides.
questions.lesson_line: Chart first. Then prefer the growing business.

wrong.The flat-sales stock; it is safer: Growth is the preference when the charts match.
wrong.Neither; fundamentals are not a factor: Growth is a preference on our list. The chart still comes first.
wrong.The grower; the chart no longer matters: Growth is a preference, not a pass on the chart. The chart still comes first.

questions.story: Two stocks hold their gap-up lows on the same day, both with strong closes and otherwise equal charts. One grows sales and earnings fast. The other has flat sales.
questions.simple: Pick the grower, because with equal charts we prefer growing sales and earnings.

deeper.trap: Growth is a preference, never a pass on the chart. If the flat-sales stock had the better chart, the chart would still come first.

questions.q: A fast-growing business can skip the chart check for Gap Support.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings, but that is a preference. The chart comes first, so a fast grower still has to pass every chart check.
questions.lesson_line: Growth is a preference. The chart comes first.
questions.simple: False. Growing sales and earnings are only preferred, and the chart always comes first.

reasons: rests on the owner's growth rule (D40)

questions.q: Bought at 27.15 with the stop at 26.89. Where is 5R?
questions.why: 28.45. One R is the fill minus the stop, 27.15 minus 26.89. Five of those above the fill is 28.45. After the first third at 3R, another third comes off at 5R, then the last third trails. GPN ran to 24.9R from these levels.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 5R before the open. The second third comes off there.
questions.simple: 5R is the fill plus five times the distance from the fill to the stop, which is 28.45.

questions.q: By default, how much of the position comes off at 5R?
choices: A third of the position
Half of the whole position
A quarter of the position
Nothing; the trail takes it
questions.answer: A third of the position
questions.why: A third of the position. By default the plan is a third at 3R, then another third at 5R, then the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: Thirds: one at 3R, one at 5R, the rest on the trail.

wrong.Half of the whole position: Half is not the plan. The plan is a third at 3R, a third at 5R, then the trail.
wrong.A quarter of the position: A quarter is not in the plan. The second trim is a third.
wrong.Nothing; the trail takes it: The trail starts after both trims, on the last third.

questions.simple: A third comes off at 5R. The default plan is a third at 3R, a third at 5R, then the last third trails.

reasons: rests on the owner's trim rule (E51, B19)

questions.q: What do you do this morning?
choices: Sell the next third at the open
Wait for a dip back to 27.05
Sell everything left at the open
Hold it all and trail the rest
questions.answer: Sell the next third at the open
questions.why: Sell the next third at the open. The stock opens at 28.20, above the 5R level of 27.05, so that trim comes off at the open. Do not wait for a dip. The last third stays on the trail.
questions.lesson_line: Gap past a trim level: take it at the open.

wrong.Wait for a dip back to 27.05: A dip may never come. A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.
wrong.Sell everything left at the open: The plan keeps the last third on the trail.
wrong.Hold it all and trail the rest: The 5R third comes off first. Only the last third trails.

questions.story: You bought at 25.10 with the stop at 24.71. The first third came off at 3R. Your 5R level is 27.05. Today the stock opens at 28.20.
questions.simple: Sell the next third at the open. A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open, and the last third trails.

reasons: rests on the owner's gap-past-a-trim rule (F63, E51)

questions.q: What do you do with your long?
choices: Sell a big part into the run
Buy more while it is strong
Hold it all and trail the 10-day
Move the stop to breakeven only
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the run
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. The story is a climax run: three up days, two gap ups, wider ranges, rising volume and a gap up today. On a climax run in your own long, we sell a big part into it. How much is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: A climax run in your own long: sell a big part into it.

wrong.Buy more while it is strong: No adding. We buy the full size at one price with one stop.
wrong.Hold it all and trail the 10-day: Trailing alone waits for the stock to turn. The rule is to sell a big part into the run.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven only: A stop at breakeven takes no profit. A climax run is when we sell a big part.

questions.story: You own a Gap Support winner up about 4R. It has risen three straight days on wider ranges and rising volume, with two gap ups in a row. Today it gaps up again.
questions.simple: Sell a big part into the run, because a climax run in your own long is when we take profit.

deeper.trap: A climax run feels like the best time to hold or add. The rulebook says the opposite: sell a big part into it. How big is a judgment call, so there is no fixed fraction to memorize.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, B26)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Before you buy, a test day that closes under the ___ is off the list.
questions.answer: 200-day
questions.why: 200-day. Before entry, a test day that closes under the 200-day is off the list. The 50-day is a check on the gap day, not the test day.
questions.lesson_line: A test day that closes under the 200-day is off the list.
questions.simple: 200-day. Before we buy, a test day that closes under the 200-day is off the list.

questions.q: What is your move today?
questions.story: You hold the last third of a steadier Gap Support winner, both trims done. Today it closes under its 10-day but still above its 21-day.
choices: Hold; the line for it is the 21-day
Sell the last third; the 10-day broke
Hold; sell if the 10-day stays broken
Sell half now and trail the rest
questions.answer: Hold; the line for it is the 21-day
questions.why: Hold. A steadier mover trails the 21-day, and we sell on a close below it. Today it closed under the 10-day but still above its 21-day. The 10-day is the fast mover's line.
questions.lesson_line: Steadier mover, 21-day line. A close under that line is the sell.

wrong.Sell the last third; the 10-day broke: The 10-day is the fast mover's trail. This steadier mover trails the 21-day.
wrong.Hold; sell if the 10-day stays broken: The 10-day is the fast mover's line. The steadier mover's line is the 21-day.
wrong.Sell half now and trail the rest: Both trims are done. The last third rides until a close under its line.

questions.simple: Hold. A steadier mover trails the 21-day and we sell on a close below it, because the 10-day is the fast mover's line.

deeper.trap: Using the fast mover's trail on a steadier winner. The 10-day is for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones. Trailing the 10-day here would sell today, while the stock's own line still holds.

reasons: rests on the owner's trail rule (E52)

questions.q: In our scan's history, most Gap Support hits reached 3R.
questions.answer: False
questions.simple: False. Only 28.9% of hits reached 3R in our scan's history, so most did not.
questions.why: False. In our scan's history, 28.9% of hits reached 3R and 20.4% reached 5R, so most did not. A past rate is not a promise for the next trade.
questions.lesson_line: A past hit rate is a base rate, not a promise.

reasons: our own scan's base rate, read from our bars (survivors only), not yet reviewed by the owner

questions.q: By our card, what does the size of this gap do to the trade?
questions.story: A leader's earnings gap closes the day 38% above the prior close. Weeks later it tests the gap-up low and closes near its high. Every other check on the card passes.
choices: It lowers the grade, but not a ban
It bans it; over 30% is never bought
It raises the grade; demand is strong
It does not count; only the test does
questions.answer: It lowers the grade, but not a ban
questions.why: It lowers the grade, but it is not a ban. On our card, a gap over 30% is a lower grade, not a ban. Wagner warns that an opening gap of more than 30% could lead to a few months of chop.
questions.lesson_line: On our card, a gap over 30% lowers the grade but does not ban the trade.

wrong.It bans it; over 30% is never bought: Our card makes a gap over 30% a lower grade, not a ban.
wrong.It raises the grade; demand is strong: It is the reverse. A gap over 30% grades lower, and Wagner warns of months of chop.
wrong.It does not count; only the test does: The gap size is part of the grade on our card, even with a clean test.

questions.simple: On our card a gap over 30 percent lowers the grade, but the trade is not banned.

reasons: proposed 30% line on the card, not yet ruled by the owner
one web source (Wagner), already checked on the page

questions.q: Why is a fixed stop 1% to 3% under the line wrong here?
questions.story: The gap-up low is the line. The test day's low dips 3.2% under it. Then the day closes back over the line in its upper half.
choices: The day already traded below it
It would sit too far from the entry
The card wants it on the line itself
Morales allows no undercut at all
questions.answer: The day already traded below it
questions.why: The day already traded below it. A stop 1% to 3% under the line sits above a low 3.2% under it. Our card proposes no fixed 1% to 3% stop, since slight breaches are often deeper. Our stop goes a few cents under the test day's low.
questions.lesson_line: The test day's real low sets the stop, not a fixed cushion under the line.

wrong.It would sit too far from the entry: It is the reverse. A 1% to 3% stop sits above this day's low, inside its range.
wrong.The card wants it on the line itself: The stop goes a few cents under the test day's low, not on the line.
wrong.Morales allows no undercut at all: Morales and Kacher say a 1 to 2% undercut can be permitted in some cases.

questions.simple: A fixed 1 to 3 percent stop sits above this day's low, so our stop goes a few cents under that low instead.

reasons: proposed criterion on the card (gs.stop_not_porosity), not yet ruled by the owner
the 3.2% dip is given in the story and sits inside the card's up-to-5% undercut allowance

questions.q: A test day that closes under the 200-day is off, even if the gap day closed above it.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The check is on the test day's close. Before entry, a test day that closes under the 200-day is off. Our rulebook takes no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: Check the 200-day on the test day's close, not the gap day's.
questions.simple: True. The test day itself must close above the 200-day, so a gap day above it does not save the trade.

questions.q: On our card, heavy-volume selling into the line is a warning, not a rule that rules out the trade.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. On our card, heavy-volume selling into the line is a warning, not a rule. A quiet pullback on lighter volume is the version traders like best.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy selling into the line is a warning. A quiet pullback on lighter volume is the one to like.
